**Verdict:** Yes. Hormozi says it may be the most powerful tactic in his ad checklist. Lead with the flaw, put "but" after it, and finish with the one claim you want believed: "[true, damaging thing] **but** [what you want them to believe]."

His reasoning is that the prospect is already thinking of your weaknesses. If you say them first, you lose a little of your promise and gain trust, so they believe the claim that follows.

**Based on:** said it (2025-05 ad-copy talk and a 2026-02 live consult)

**Why he'd say it**
- He rates it above everything else: "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions" ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=750s)). "of course your product isn't perfect say so" (@ 12:30).
- Trust matters more than the size of the promise: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" ([@ 13:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)).
- Honesty stands out because competitors won't do it: "if you want to stand out in a crowded marketplace tell the truth" ([@ 15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)). "anyone can say" yours is the most fun gym, "but what people won't say is the truth" ([@ 16:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=975s)).

**How to word it (his method)**
1. **List the flaws.** "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([@ 15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)). His reason is that "the prospect is already thinking them" (@ 15:39).
2. **Put the flaw first and the claim after "but".** "the statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" ([@ 13:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=824s)). He warns that reversing the order backfires. With "these markers write four times longer than others but they smell like crap", he says you end up "emphasizing the fact that they smell bad" ([@ 14:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=866s)).
3. **Copy the shape of his examples:**
   - "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" (@ 15:03)
   - "our systems are incredibly boring but they work" (@ 15:03)
   - "listen our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's cuz it's all we've got" (@ 15:39)
4. **Use humor if you can.** "if you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" (@ 15:39). He also calls humor the first thing he'd cut, so it's optional.
5. **If the offer sounds too good to be true, make it sound less good.** "when you even offer this too good to be true, you make it less good. So that it's more believable." ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 19:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1149s)). For sales calls or longer copy he scripts it as: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad." ([@ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s)). Then you list the downsides as reasons it won't work for some people ("you can have what you want, just not when you want"), "So then they can self-qualify." ([@ 20:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1214s)). The prospects who stay don't object, because "They want it. They just don't believe it." ([@ 20:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1247s)).

A fill-in version for your ad:
> "Honestly, [thing people complain about]. And [second complaint]. But [the one result you want them to believe]."

**Which flaws to pick** (follows from what he said, confidence: medium): pick ones that are real, that buyers already worry about, and that don't undercut the claim after "but". His examples give up something peripheral (parking, looks, smell, boredom) to protect the core result (fun sessions, conversions, ink life). The flaw also does a second job: it calls out who the product isn't for, which he says "is actually even more powerful than the original call out" (@ 5:02).

**What he's done:** He calls his own companies' websites "ugly as hell but they convert". In the 2026 consult he had a travel-points coaching business open its sales calls with the downsides, because its testimonials were being called fake.

**What would change his answer:** The vault has nothing where he advises against it. The method only works if the flaw is true and leaves the "but" claim standing. If your weakness is the very result you're promising (slow results when speed is the pitch), it doesn't fit his examples. Fix the offer first, which is his rule whenever too few people say yes.

One caveat on the evidence: his support is unnamed research on admitting bias plus anecdotes like the Eminem rap battle. The vault has no A/B numbers from him. In his own spirit, run it as a test against your current ad rather than taking it on faith.

**Verdict:** Hormozi says 20% monthly churn is average for a paid community, under 10% is the best groups, and you should make retention your top priority once churn passes 30%, meaning fewer than 7 in 10 members stay each month. Watch churn by cohort, though, not as one blended average. Members almost always leave fastest in months 1–3, so high month-one churn alone isn't a reason to panic.

**Based on:** said it. He covers this directly in one 2026 talk, ["How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q), using platform averages from Skool.

**The benchmarks**
- **Average:** 80% stay each month, so 20% churn. **Best:** under 10% churn. **Not good:** under 70% retention, so churn of 30% or more ([@ 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s)).
- **When to worry:** "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." (@ 1:39)
- **Why it matters:** going from 20% to 10% churn "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" ([@ 2:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=133s)).

**When to worry, and when not to**
- **Track joins against cancels every month.** "track those two numbers on a monthly basis, joins versus cancels, and then force yourself to label the businesses growing, flat, or declining" ([@ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=33s)). You're shrinking when more members cancel than join.
- **Expect churn to fall with tenure.** "the biggest rule is that churn drops dramatically with time" ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=199s)). His platform averages:
  - Months 1–3: 20%+ churn.
  - After day 90: "it drops to around 10% or less."
  - By month six: "it goes from like 10% to 2%." ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s))
- **The real warning signs, by his numbers:** members who have passed day 90 still leaving at well over 10% a month, or members past month six leaving at well over 2%.
- **Month one alone isn't a warning sign.** "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks" ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s)). The exception is "unless basically everyone's leaving, in which case, yes, you should go fix that" ([@ 4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=297s)).
- **A young community will look worse than it is.** If it's under 90 days old, your churn "is always going to be inflated" because nobody has reached the low-churn months yet (@ 4:24).

**What he'd have you work on instead of "the number"**
- He reframes the goal: not "How do I make this number go down?" but "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" (@ 4:24)
- **Month one:** "have a very specific strategy for getting people past the first month cuz that's the biggest month of churn" (@ 4:57). That means onboarding, setting expectations and showing up daily. He also says to "pin the fast win up front so new members hit that value ideally within the first 24 hours" ([@ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=786s)).
- **Day 90 and month six:** "Day 90 is probably going to have to deliver some sort of outcome, some sort of change in behavior for them. Month six, it's usually them connecting with other people within that community." ([@ 5:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=331s))
- **Find out why people leave:** "for every 20 cancels or so, review the top one or two reasons, and then fix those" ([@ 6:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=395s)). Ask your longest-staying members why they stay, too.
- **Offer less, not more:** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm." ([@ 9:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s))

**What he's done:** He admits he used to obsess over his average monthly churn number before switching to the day-90 and month-six framing (@ 3:53).

**What would change his answer:**
- His benchmarks are for online and consumer services. He says they don't apply to things like "an insurance premium or an alarm system" ([@ 1:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=65s)).
- The vault has only this one source on churn, and the numbers come from Skool, a platform he promotes and talks about as "us". Take that into account when weighing them.

**Verdict:** Pay it off fast, on a fixed schedule of a few months, and don't treat it as debt *versus* growth. In a case almost identical to yours (a profitable service business with $60k of debt) Hormozi approved the owner's plan to clear it in 4–5 months. He put "keep paying the debt" second on the priority list, after a price rise and ahead of everything else. The growth moves he leads with cost very little cash.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed nearly this exact situation in his May 2026 consult with Corey, who runs ProShine, an HVAC duct-cleaning business.

**Why he'd say it**
- **He leans toward paying debt off.** His first question about Corey's debt was "how fast you plan on paying off the 60k debt that you have." When Corey said four to five months, he answered "Okay, good." and added: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s).
- **His one argument is risk.** "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." and "businesses have seasons, they have volatility". He also points at why people borrow: "A lot of times it's like cuz I wanted to grow faster." His example of an enduring company: "a lot of like Chick-fil-A operate debt free." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s)
- **He admits it isn't mainly a financial lever.** "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." (@ 8:37). Later he puts the profit gain from being debt-free at about 5%, and the turn that follows seems to be his: "But at least 100% in headache." (@ 32:53, speaker attribution medium confidence).
- **His growth plan doesn't need the debt money.** In order, his list was: raise prices 10%, "continue to pay off the debt", fix the landing page, fix the ads, and only then spend more on ads ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s). He explains the order: "if we fix the landing page and we just improve the ads you have you might already double or triple your lead flow. And so, you might not even have to spend more" (@ 31:48). His framing for a business that already works: "Like no Hail Mary's. This is just consistent yardage." (@ 4:19)
- **His exception is ad spend with proven returns.** "we just want to continue to spend month over month provided our ROAS and our CAC stay more or less the same." (@ 10:48). "If you know that's where the money's coming from, by all means, spend more." But: "if you're not sure, then you have a data problem." (@ 11:21). Corey's ads were returning 13:1, and Hormozi still had him keep paying down the debt while he scaled. He funded both from profit and didn't choose between them.

**What he's done:** He endorsed paying the $60k off over 4–5 months while cutting nothing from the growth plan. A year later Corey reported projecting $2.3–2.5M in revenue, up from $1.25M. The follow-up doesn't say whether the debt was cleared.

**What would change his answer**
- **Cash flow.** Corey's $60k was roughly six weeks of his $479k annual profit. If $60k is most of your cash buffer, emptying it all at once could leave you exposed to the same "seasons" and "volatility" his argument is about. That's my extrapolation, not something he said. His approach still points to steady, aggressive monthly payments rather than keeping the debt.
- **A channel with proven, attributed returns.** He'd put cash behind that, but alongside the payoff, not in place of it.
- **His own inconsistency.** Elsewhere he argues that most entrepreneurs take too little risk, and he describes heavy debt as how private-equity fund managers get "mega rich" ([[yt-rMJIOK_FgJk]] @ 15:51; [[yt-sL16tsGafcQ]] @ 18:02). He never reconciles this with his debt aversion. For an operating service business, though, his only direct advice is the Ramsey-leaning view.

One note of my own: he never mentions interest rates. If your $60k is expensive debt (credit cards, a merchant cash advance), paying it off is an even clearer call. If it's a cheap, long-term loan, his case rests on the risk and "headache" argument, which he himself calls emotional.

I can save this answer as `derived/pay-off-debt-or-grow.md` if you'd like to keep it.

**Verdict:** No, don't hold your prices. Hormozi would have you raise them about 10% now. He reads a close rate above 80% as a sign you're underpriced, and he gave this exact advice to a duct-cleaning owner with almost exactly your numbers.

His reasoning is that for an ordinary home service, a higher price makes customers more confident you'll deliver, so the close rate can hold or even go up. The math works even if it drops. At a 38% margin, a 10% raise makes more money as long as you still close more than about 65%.

**Based on:** said it. In May 2026 he did a consult with Corey, who owns ProShine, a duct-cleaning company. ProShine had $1.25M in trailing revenue, a 38% net margin and an 82% close rate ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4)). All quotes below come from that consult (`yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4`).

**Why he'd say it**
- **An 82% close rate means you're underpriced:** "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." ([@ 8:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
- **Where it stops paying off:** "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." He estimated the 10% raise at "roughly a 25% increase in net profit" at the same volume (@ 8:06). For you that's about $120K added to roughly $456K of profit, or +26%.
- **A higher price builds trust:** "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([@ 7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)) He says this isn't a luxury effect, since nobody brags about what they paid for their HVAC. It's trust. Priced too low, you look like a "super seedy duct tape operation" (@ 7:33).
- **The bigger risk is being afraid to charge:** "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" ([@ 7:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)). For businesses under about $3–5M, he calls charging more "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business" (@ 8:06).
- **He shares your worry about breaking something, and still put price first.** He said "The last thing I want to do is like break something" and "Like no Hail Mary's. This is just consistent yardage." ([@ 4:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=259s)). Then he made pricing #1 of his six fixes. His answer to that worry is a small raise, not no raise. He called it "more asking than telling" (@ 8:06): you try it and watch the numbers.

**What he's done**
- His Acquisition.com team had already told Corey the business was underpriced compared with others in the space. Corey raised prices 23%, which "resulted in a higher close rate and more money" ([@ 6:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=386s)). The 82% close rate came after that raise, and Hormozi still pushed another 10%, to about $1,650 per unit.
- He tied the higher price to a stronger savings pitch: show customers their energy bills before and after, so the job pays for itself in about 18 months (@ 17:45).
- At the one-year follow-up, Corey said he was on track for $2.3–2.5M, up from $1.25M. He credited marketing, the landing page and more ad spend, and didn't say what the second raise did to the close rate.

**What would change his answer:** your close rate after the raise. If it falls toward his 65% line, you've gone too far. He also says the close rate only "sometimes" goes up, so treat it as a test.

**My own arithmetic (not in the vault):** His 65% treats your whole 38% margin as the profit on each job. If a lot of your costs are fixed (salaried crews, vans, office), each job earns more than 38% and the break-even is higher. At a 50% per-job margin, it's about 68%. That's still well under 82%.

**Where I'd push back:** the claim that a raise actually increases close rate rests on one owner's own report. The stronger argument is the break-even math, which works even if your close rate drops somewhat.

**This isn't Hormozi's story. It's Steven Bartlett's.** It comes from Hormozi's Diary of a CEO episode (E235, 3 April 2023, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo)). Bartlett, the host, tells it about his own career, and Hormozi responds to it. None of Hormozi's companies has gone public. The transcript is auto-captions with no speaker labels, so I worked out who's talking from context. Bartlett says his company "went public on a Stock Exchange in … Europe" and then names Flight Story, the company he co-founded. The vault's wiki also leaves this passage out of Hormozi's statements.

**Bartlett's story**

1. **The NASDAQ point** ([@ 1:34:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s)): After his company listed in Europe, he met about 20 investment banks while considering an IPO in another country. They told him "if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more which meant that my net worth would be [4x] just by taking the exact same business and moving it to a different Stock Exchange." (The company was Social Chain, which listed in Germany. That detail isn't in the vault.)
2. **What he took from it:** "you have to not just have the skill but know what Market to apply it to." He went looking for the industry where his social media and storytelling skills were scarcest and paid most. His answer was companies about to IPO, because "if you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions."
3. **The equity deal** ([@ 1:35:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5717s)): He framed the choice as helping "a local gym and get paid a [$1,000]" or helping a company in the run-up to an IPO. The first one he worked with listed "at 3 billion." He was paid in equity, and "on the day of the IPO the equity that I got for for the 9 to 12 months work that i' done was worth in the region of 7 to8 million," which he called "basically freelance." He says that's why he started Flight Story, which began in the IPO market.

**Hormozi's response**

- He agreed ("100% I thoroughly agree") and moved to his own theme: "the biggest debt all of us pay is ignorance" ([@ 1:36:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5818s)). He tied it to a closer's pitch he once watched: someone earning $50,000 is "paying" life $950,000 a year for not knowing how to make $1M.
- He compared it to fishing: anyone can drop a hook in the water, but good fishermen know where the fish are. Bartlett had the same rod and went where the best fishing was.
- His own version is conversion-rate work ([@ 1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)): "I do the same work to a business doing $100 million a year I make them $20 million for my 20% bump and I get 10% that and I make $2 million 20,000 2 million 100x same work." He followed with "solve rich people problems they pay better."

The vault files this under `wiki/pricing/premium-pricing/sell-to-customers-who-value-it-most.md`. Bartlett's lines are quoted from the raw transcript (`raw/yt-x3e73Qn6NOo.md`, roughly lines 429–447).

**He didn't say that. He said the opposite.** In the vault's only roofing consult, with Caleb of Keys Roofing in St. Louis, Hormozi told him to go *all in* on door-knocking. He never told him to move money into Google Ads.

**Verdict:** Keep knocking doors, and scale it by building a door-to-door sales team. His reasoning: a tiny business has little time or money, so every dollar should go to the highest-return channel the owner has already proven. For Caleb that was knocking doors, where about one in 20 closed.

**Based on:** said it. The consult is "How I Would Build a $10M Service Business" (2026-08, [yt-o64cI6tebnU](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU)).

**What he actually told him**
- **Focus the few resources he has.** "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([@ 3:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s))
- **Being able to go get a sale on demand is rare.** "that reliability of being able to just basically go get money um is something that a lot of entrepreneurs don't know how to do." (@ 3:16) He said it gives an entrepreneur extra lives, like a cat's nine.
- **Don't get clever.** "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([@ 9:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s)) "It's what you're good at." "Like I don't think we need to be cute about this." ([@ 10:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=621s))
- **Scale it with reps paid per door.** A 10% commission on a $4K repair, spread over about 50 doors, is roughly $10 a door: "want to go make 10 bucks? Knock that door." "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." ([@ 10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=654s)) "DDD" is the auto-caption for "D2D".
- **He repeated it in his recap:** "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." ([@ 24:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1467s))

This fits his general habits: find the constraint, do one thing, and improve what already works before adding a channel. In another consult he said "New channel, little too hard for right now in my opinion." ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1446s) @ 24:06)

**Where the Google Ads idea may come from:** a different consult. Corey runs ProShine, an HVAC-duct cleaning business doing about $1.25M a year ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4), 2026-05). Corey said about 60% of his leads already came from paid ads, with $3K–5K a month going to Google. Hormozi's advice there was to scale ads that were already returning: "If you answer that correctly, the answer would be as many dollars as you possibly could." ([@ 11:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=681s)) He made that conditional on trustworthy attribution, and he wanted the landing page and ad creative fixed before more spend. He never mentioned door-knocking in that consult.

**What would change his answer:** proof that a paid channel returns more than door-knocking, with attribution he trusts. His rule is to back whatever channel already has proven returns. For Caleb at two months old, that channel was door-to-door.

In the 90-day follow-up, Caleb said he went all in on door-knocking and that revenue went from a little under $32K to about $247K. Those are his own figures, and the video doesn't say whether they're monthly or cumulative.
